subtype: Observer of a very open peer [Observer]
passage:
Pema has lived in four cities since I met her, and this year alone she's taken up pottery, Portuguese and a podcast about bridges. At our design firm in Pune, half the team loves her pitches. The other half rolls their eyes: "Another Pema idea, gone by Friday." I used to be in the second half. Then I watched her, in a client meeting, pull a solution out of something she'd learned in pottery class, and nobody else in that room could have made the leap. Still, her half-finished decks pile up. Last month I offered to be her "Friday person": she brings me one idea, and we write three next steps together. Two of them are already live.
Jomon

qa.q: What three things has Pema taken up this year?
qa.a: Pottery, Portuguese and a podcast about bridges.

qa.q: What changed Jomon's mind about Pema, and what does it suggest Jomon now believes?
qa.a: Watching her pull a client solution out of pottery class showed Jomon that her wide interests can produce ideas nobody else reaches.

qa.q: What choice did Jomon make to help Pema's ideas get finished?
qa.a: Jomon offered to be her "Friday person", turning one idea a week into three written next steps, and two are already live.

qa.q: How might Pema feel about the half of the team that rolls their eyes?
qa.a: She may feel misjudged as flaky when her curiosity is where her best ideas come from, and she may welcome help that shows her follow-through.

grounding: A colleague watches a friend who keeps changing cities and hobbies, sees both fresh thinking and flakiness in others' eyes, and helps with follow-through.

subtype: Observer of a very open peer [Observer]
passage:
Peer-mentor note, 12 August. Urmila, same team
Shankar and I became friends the week he joined, eight months ago, from a startup in Kochi; before that, a bakery; before that, a year of teaching in Ladakh. In meetings he throws out three new ideas an hour. Some colleagues find it energising. One told me privately that he is "a flake who won't last the year." I don't agree with either extreme. His idea of reading circles at the bus depot is the best thing we have tried. But his project tracker has six rows marked "started" and none marked "done". Today I asked him to pick one idea to finish before starting any new ones. He chose the bus depot. We will check in each Monday.

qa.q: Where did Shankar teach for a year?
qa.a: He spent a year of teaching in Ladakh.

qa.q: What does Urmila seem to think of the colleague's "flake" remark?
qa.a: Urmila seems uneasy with it and finds it unfair and too extreme, since Shankar's bus depot idea is the best thing they have tried.

qa.q: What choice did Urmila make after looking at the tracker?
qa.a: Urmila asked Shankar to pick one idea to finish before any new ones and set Monday check-ins.

qa.q: How might the colleague who called Shankar a flake see him if the bus depot circles get finished?
qa.a: They might start to see his openness as useful rather than flaky, once one of his ideas reaches "done".

grounding: A colleague and friend watches a very open teammate whom some find energising and others flaky, and helps him turn an idea into follow-through.
